name: IL-1α
source: Epithelial cells and tissue macrophages
trigger: Cell damage or necrosis releases IL-1α already present inside many tissue cells.
target: Endothelium, fibroblasts and immune cells
action: Activates nearby cells to produce inflammatory mediators and adhesion molecules. Blood-vessel lining becomes more able to recruit circulating white blood cells.
gut: At a damaged gut surface, IL-1α helps turn tissue injury into an immune response. IL-1Ra blocks the receptor used by both IL-1α and IL-1β.

name: IL-1β
source: Monocytes, macrophages and other activated cells
trigger: Microbial sensing increases production of inactive pro-IL-1β. Inflammasome activation can then activate caspase-1, which cuts it into a mature cytokine.
target: Immune cells, endothelium and nerve-associated tissues
action: Promotes fever, inflammatory mediator production and increased pain sensitivity. Production and activation are separate steps: having the precursor does not mean mature IL-1β has been released.
gut: Microbial products and damaged tissue can feed this pathway. In the pain story, IL-1β connects immune activation with changes in how pain pathways respond.

name: IL-1Ra
source: Monocytes, macrophages and other tissue cells
trigger: Inflammatory stimulation and feedback signals, including IL-6 in human infusion experiments, can increase IL-1Ra production.
target: Cells that would otherwise respond to IL-1α or IL-1β
action: Binds IL-1R1 without recruiting the accessory protein needed to start IL-1 signalling. IL-1α and IL-1β therefore have fewer available receptors to activate.
gut: This is a direct example of an inflammatory response recruiting its own inhibition. IL-1Ra is a naturally produced protein; anakinra is a recombinant medicine based on it.

name: TNF-α
source: Activated macrophages, T cells and other immune cells
trigger: Recognition of microbes and activation of immune cells stimulate TNF production; membrane TNF can be cleaved into a soluble form.
target: Blood-vessel lining, immune cells and intestinal tissue
pathway: NF-κB / MAPK; cell-death pathways in some settings
action: Makes blood vessels more receptive to white-cell recruitment and stimulates inflammatory gene expression. Receptor and cellular state determine whether signalling supports survival or contributes to cell death.
gut: Persistent TNF activity can contribute to intestinal tissue damage. Anti-TNF medicines are established treatments for selected patients with IBD, connecting this signalling pathway to clinical care.

name: IL-6
source: Macrophages, stromal cells and exercising muscle
trigger: Microbial sensing, tissue injury and other cytokines stimulate production. Contracting muscle also releases IL-6 during exercise.
target: Liver cells, immune cells and other responsive tissues
action: Stimulates liver production of acute-phase proteins such as CRP and changes immune-cell behaviour. Soluble IL-6 receptor can extend responsiveness to cells carrying gp130.
gut: IL-6 links local inflammation to whole-body responses. In a human experiment, IL-6 infusion increased IL-10 and IL-1Ra, showing a route from an activating signal into regulatory feedback.

sources.title: IL-6 increases IL-10 and IL-1Ra in humans

name: IL-8 / CXCL8
source: Stimulated epithelial cells, macrophages and endothelium
trigger: Microbial products and cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF stimulate CXCL8 release.
target: Neutrophils
action: Creates a chemical gradient that neutrophils can follow towards a site of infection or damage. It also helps activate these cells when they arrive. CXCL8 is a chemokine: a cytokine specialised in directing cell movement.
gut: At intestinal or lung surfaces, recruited neutrophils can kill microbes but also release enzymes and oxidants that injure tissue. Recruitment is a concrete mechanism connecting cytokines to local damage.

sources.title: IL-8 / CXCL8 · protein function and signalling (UniProt)

outcome: Neutrophils arrive at the responding site

name: IL-10
source: Regulatory T cells, macrophages, B cells and other lymphocytes
trigger: Microbial stimulation and immune activation recruit IL-10-producing responses alongside inflammatory pathways.
target: Macrophages, dendritic cells and other immune cells
action: Reduces production of inflammatory mediators and limits antigen-presenting cell activation. This helps prevent a defensive response from continually amplifying itself.
gut: Gut immune cells encounter microbial material every day. IL-10 helps contain their response; mice lacking IL-10 develop chronic enterocolitis, while human IL-10 pathway defects can cause very early-onset IBD.

name: IL-17A
source: Th17 cells, γδ T cells and group 3 innate lymphoid cells
trigger: IL-1 and IL-23 support responses from IL-17-producing cells; antigen recognition also activates Th17 cells.
target: Epithelial and stromal cells
action: Induces chemokines and antimicrobial responses in tissue cells. It often works with TNF to increase signals that recruit neutrophils.
gut: Supports defence against extracellular bacteria and fungi at barriers. Blocking IL-17A failed in a Crohn’s trial: removing an inflammatory signal can also remove useful intestinal defence.

name: IL-17F
source: Th17 cells and innate lymphocytes
trigger: Inflammatory and antigen-driven activation of IL-17-producing lymphocytes.
target: Epithelial and stromal cells
action: Promotes epithelial inflammatory mediators and neutrophil-recruiting signals. IL-17F can act as a paired IL-17F molecule or pair with IL-17A.
gut: IL-17A and IL-17F share receptors and some functions but are separate proteins. Keeping them distinct makes studies of barrier inflammation and cytokine-targeted medicines easier to understand.

name: IL-23
source: Activated dendritic cells and macrophages
trigger: Microbial recognition at tissue surfaces stimulates antigen-presenting cells to produce IL-23.
target: Th17 cells and other IL-23-responsive lymphocytes
action: Supports expansion and inflammatory activity of type 17 lymphocytes, which can produce IL-17 and IL-22. IL-23 contains p19 and p40 subunits; p40 is shared with IL-12.
gut: IL-23 is a major link between microbial sensing and sustained intestinal immune responses. Experimental intestinal inflammation and clinical targeting of this pathway make it central to the IBD story.

name: IL-22
role: Act directly on the epithelial barrier
source: Group 3 innate lymphoid cells, Th17 and Th22 cells
trigger: Signals including IL-23 activate IL-22-producing lymphocytes.
target: Intestinal and other epithelial cells
action: Stimulates antimicrobial proteins, epithelial survival and tissue regeneration. Its main targets are barrier cells rather than the immune cells that produce it.
gut: This closes a useful loop: immune cells detect a problem, then tell the intestinal lining to strengthen defence and repair. Mouse experiments link epithelial STAT3 to IL-22-dependent mucosal healing.

sources.title: IL-22, STAT3 and mucosal wound healing

name: IL-12
source: Dendritic cells and macrophages
trigger: Microbial recognition and interactions with activated T cells increase IL-12 production.
target: Natural killer cells and T cells
action: Promotes IFN-γ production and differentiation of helper T cells towards a Th1 response. This helps organise defence against pathogens living inside cells.
gut: IL-12 and IL-23 share p40 but activate different receptor complexes. This distinction explains how one molecular target can affect more than one intestinal immune pathway.

name: IFN-γ
source: Natural killer cells, Th1 cells and cytotoxic T cells
trigger: IL-12 and IL-18 stimulate innate production; antigen recognition stimulates activated T cells.
target: Macrophages, epithelial cells and other nucleated cells
action: Increases macrophage antimicrobial activity and antigen presentation. It changes how infected cells and neighbouring tissue participate in cellular immunity.
gut: The gut needs this machinery to control invasive pathogens. Sustained activation can also contribute to epithelial dysfunction and intestinal inflammation.

name: IFN-α / IFN-β
source: Virus-sensing cells; plasmacytoid dendritic cells are major IFN-α producers
trigger: Recognition of viral nucleic acids by cellular sensors triggers type I interferon production.
target: Infected and neighbouring cells
action: Switches on interferon-stimulated genes that interfere with viral replication and spread. Neighbouring cells can prepare antiviral machinery before becoming infected.
gut: An important bridge between gut and respiratory infection: antiviral protection involves a different programme from simply recruiting inflammatory cells. Type I interferons and IFN-γ use different receptors.

sources.title: IFN-α / IFN-β · protein function and signalling (UniProt)

name: IL-2
role: Expand T cells and maintain regulation
source: Activated T cells
trigger: Antigen recognition together with co-stimulation induces IL-2 release.
target: Activated T cells and regulatory T cells
action: Supports T-cell proliferation. Regulatory T cells express a high-affinity IL-2 receptor that helps them obtain the IL-2 needed for survival and suppressive function.
gut: Intestinal immunity needs both responsive T cells and cells that restrain them. IL-2 feeds both sides of that organisation through receptor expression and local availability.

name: IL-4
source: Th2 cells, basophils and other activated immune cells
trigger: Allergen- and parasite-associated responses activate IL-4-producing cells.
receptor: IL-4Rα + common γ chain or IL-13Rα1
target: T cells, B cells and tissue cells
action: Promotes Th2 differentiation and antibody switching towards IgE. It also changes macrophage behaviour and works with IL-13 in type 2 responses.
gut: Provides a route into intestinal worm defence and allergic disease. This is a different immune programme from the IL-12–IFN-γ response to intracellular pathogens.

name: IL-5
source: Th2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells
trigger: Type 2 responses, including stimulation by epithelial alarm signals, increase IL-5 production.
target: Eosinophil precursors and mature eosinophils
pathway: JAK / STAT and other survival pathways
action: Promotes eosinophil development, activation and survival. Eosinophils contain granules whose contents can act against parasites and damage host tissue.
gut: Connects parasite defence with eosinophilic inflammation in the digestive tract and airways. It supplies a different kind of cellular reinforcement from CXCL8-driven neutrophil recruitment.

name: IL-13
role: Increase mucus and alter barrier tissue
source: Th2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells
trigger: Type 2 immune activation, including signals from IL-25 and IL-33, stimulates production.
target: Epithelial cells, smooth muscle and stromal cells
action: Promotes mucus-producing cell responses and alters tissue function, including smooth-muscle activity. Prolonged activity can contribute to tissue remodelling.
gut: Mucus and intestinal contraction help expel worms. Related tissue programmes contribute to mucus production and airway dysfunction in allergic lung disease.

name: IL-18
source: Macrophages and epithelial cells
trigger: Inactive pro-IL-18 can be cleaved by caspase-1 after inflammasome activation.
target: Natural killer cells and T cells
action: Works with IL-12 to stimulate IFN-γ production. IL-18-binding protein captures released IL-18 and limits the amount available to its receptor.
gut: Links intracellular danger sensing in intestinal cells to lymphocyte responses. IL-18 and IL-1β can share an activation enzyme while producing different downstream effects.

name: IL-33
source: Epithelial, endothelial and stromal cells
trigger: Tissue injury can release IL-33 from cells where it is normally associated with the nucleus.
target: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells, mast cells and some T cells
action: Activates cells that produce IL-5 and IL-13, connecting barrier injury to eosinophil and mucus responses. It also participates in tissue repair programmes.
gut: A useful gut–lung connection: both surfaces contain cells able to turn injury into type 2 immune activation. Soluble ST2 can capture IL-33 before it reaches cell-bound receptors.

name: IL-25 / IL-17E
source: Epithelial cells, including intestinal tuft cells
trigger: Tuft cells can detect intestinal parasites and release IL-25 as part of an epithelial sensing response.
target: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells and other responsive cells
action: Stimulates ILC2 production of IL-5 and IL-13. IL-13 then increases epithelial tuft and goblet cell responses, forming a feedback circuit for worm expulsion.
gut: Despite belonging to the IL-17 family, IL-25 drives a type 2 programme rather than the same response as IL-17A. Family names alone do not tell you the biological effect.

sources.title: IL-25 / IL-17E · protein function and signalling (UniProt)

name: TGF-β1
role: Regulate T cells and tissue repair
source: Regulatory T cells, macrophages, platelets and tissue cells
trigger: Produced in a latent complex that must be activated locally, for example through integrin-mediated processes.
target: Immune cells, fibroblasts and epithelial cells
action: Contributes to regulatory T-cell development and tissue repair. It also stimulates extracellular-matrix production by fibroblasts; persistent activity can contribute to fibrosis.
gut: Connects immune tolerance to the physical structure of gut tissue. Repair includes rebuilding a barrier, but excessive matrix deposition can stiffen and narrow tissue.

name: IL-7
source: Stromal and epithelial cells
trigger: Steady tissue production supports lymphocyte maintenance; availability changes with tissue state and the number of consuming cells.
target: Developing and mature T cells and some innate lymphoid cells
action: Provides survival signals that maintain immune-cell populations between episodes of infection. It helps determine which cells are available when a response begins.
gut: The immune system at a barrier is maintained continuously. IL-7 illustrates the supporting biology underneath more visible inflammatory cytokine bursts.

name: IL-15
role: Support NK and memory CD8 T cells
source: Dendritic cells, monocytes and tissue cells
trigger: Microbial and inflammatory stimulation can increase IL-15 availability on producing cells.
receptor: IL-15Rα presents IL-15 to IL-2Rβ / common γ chain
target: Natural killer cells and memory CD8 T cells
action: Often delivered across direct cell contact: IL-15 bound to IL-15Rα on one cell stimulates receptor components on a neighbouring lymphocyte. Supports survival and cytotoxic responses.
gut: Shows that immune messages need not diffuse freely through blood. Local IL-15 signalling can shape intestinal lymphocytes and contributes to the immune biology of coeliac disease.

name: IL-21
source: Activated helper T cells, particularly follicular helper T cells
trigger: Antigen-driven T-cell activation and helper-cell differentiation induce IL-21 production.
target: B cells and several T-cell populations
action: Helps B cells differentiate into antibody-producing cells and shapes helper T-cell responses. Its effects depend on the other signals arriving at the same cell.
gut: Connects intestinal adaptive immunity with antibody responses and inflammatory T-cell circuits. It adds the B-cell branch that a macrophage-only picture would miss.

name: GM-CSF
source: Activated T cells, innate lymphoid cells and tissue cells
trigger: Inflammatory or tissue-derived stimulation induces granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor.
target: Monocytes, macrophages and granulocyte-lineage cells
action: Supports survival and activation of myeloid cells. In the lungs it is required for normal alveolar macrophage function and handling of surfactant.
gut: Adds an important gut–lung distinction: cytokines shape the resident cells that maintain each organ, as well as recruiting new cells during inflammation.

name: CCL2 / MCP-1
source: Activated macrophages, endothelium, fibroblasts and epithelial cells
trigger: Tissue injury and inflammatory signals such as TNF stimulate chemokine production.
target: Circulating monocytes
action: Helps monocytes leave circulation and enter responding tissue, where they can become macrophages or related inflammatory cells.
gut: Complements CXCL8: different chemokines recruit different cells. Monocyte recruitment is one route by which an intestinal or lung response changes its cellular composition.

sources.title: CCL2 / MCP-1 · protein function and signalling (UniProt)
